content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper proposes lattice convolutional networks for learning ground states of quantum many body systems. In order to accommodate non-square lattices, a grid-like augmentation with non-uniform padding is performed to enable regular convolution. Experiments compare performance with existing approaches based on graph neural networks.

The reviewers found the paper to be clearly written and easy to read. They also agree that the LCN architecture has numerous benefits, including the ability to efficiently utilize hardware, favorable performance relative to GNN on many tasks, and overall simplicity. The framing of the paper, however, does not clearly draw out these benefits; instead, there are a variety of claims which some reviewers found unconvincing and unsupported by evidence.

One such claim is that the LCN is generic whereas the GNN needs quantum physics knowledge. The paper would benefit from a narrower and more precise version of this statement, as it came up in the discussion but remains a point of confusion. Another such claim concerns the equal or better performance of LCN vs GNN, which at least some reviewers found to be wanting in evidence.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: While the reviewers do acknowledge that this paper makes important contributions, there are lingering concerns about the structural comparison with GNNs, as well as the ultimate performance benefits of LCNs.

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
> But more importantly, regular convolution can find more useful patterns (local spin interactions) instead of just looking at unit cell.
I'm not sure I understand your claim here. I think having specialized weights (either via fixed convolutional kernel in LCN, or node features in GNN) achieves this, so it is a feature of both architectures?

To put it in other words, I believe that by introducing connections between more distant nodes on the graph (between all nodes that fall under the LCN kernel) one could instantiate an LCN in a GNN setting (by having convolutions carried out as message passing, modulo additional auxiliary nodes introduced by construction).

In this sense it feels strange to me to say that LCN is a principled way of doing this...

content.title: Reply to Q2 disagreement
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback, we would like to share our thoughts on these comments.

1. Yes, GNNs in their default instantiation are not universal function approximators. This is also mentioned in the GNN paper [1] appendix c as an alternative view of why using sublattice encoding. They use sublattice encoding to slightly break the spatial symmetry of the original GNN to make GNN more expressive. And sublattice encodings break the symmetry of GNN in a way that consistent with the underlying symmetry of the structre.

2. Sublattice encoding in GNN is inspired by regular states [2]. First, in [2], it says these regular states depend on lattice point symmetry and spin symmetry, and **these states are good "variational candidates" to the ground state of many specific models**. Second, in GNN paper, for one type lattice, it uses different sublattice encoding for different interaction strength value in Hamiltonian, which **implies that choice of sublattice encoding depends on the underlying quantm physics systems**. Based on these facts, to out best knowledge, we think sublattice encodings not only use some algebraic symmetry groups knowledge, but also more or less consider some quantum knowledge. 

3. Sorry for causing the confusion. By "lattice symmetry", we actually refer to lattice point group symmetry and translation symmetry is not an element of point group symmetry. But yes, we do consider translation symmetry by using periodic padding in lattice convolution. The reason is that we want to make it consistent with the periodic boundary condition of the lattice system, which is defined in the Hamiltonian of the system when evaluating local energy. And we do observe that this simple periodic padding will help learn more accurate ground state.

4. About unit cell, sublattice encodings do denotes the node’s location in a unit cell. And we agree that in LCN, regular convolution on augmented lattices will also capture unit cell of original lattice. But more importantly, regular convolution can find more useful patterns (local spin interactions) instead of just looking at unit cell. And the way of adding virtual vertices is just to make augmented lattice has same local structure everywhere so regular kernel can be applied. Then we can overlap the same convolution kernel in order to enable information reuse, which is crucial to capture long-range spin correlations and hence to learn accurate ground state [3]. 

**Reference**\
[1] Dmitrii Kochkov, Tobias Pfaff, Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez, Peter Battaglia, and Bryan K Clark. Learning ground states of quantum hamiltonians with graph networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.06390, 2021.\
[2] Messio, L., C. Lhuillier, and G. Misguich. "Lattice symmetries and regular states in classical frustrated antiferromagnets."\
[3] Xiao Liang, Wen-Yuan Liu, Pei-Ze Lin, Guang-Can Guo, Yong-Sheng Zhang, and Lixin He. Solving frustrated quantum many-particle models with convolutional neural networks. Physical Review B, 98(10):104426, 2018.

content.title: Q2 disagreement
content.comment:
Thank you for your updates, however I politely disagree with your statement regarding Q2:

> First, since GNN cannot capture structure information naturally, so it need to explicitly design sublattice encoding as auxiliary input according to lattice point group symmetry.
I'm not sure I understand this statement (i.e. "capture structure information naturally"); I could hypothesis that authors mean that GNNs in their default instantiation are not universal function approximators, because the structure of the point group of the lattice [1]. (if this wasn't the case, then GNNs would be arguably a better choice as it respects more spatial symmetries than convolution based approach).

> And in pratice GNN sublattice encoding need to be specifically designed for different Hamiltonian (different J2 value) and different lattice types, so it indeed need quantum physics knowledge involved and not generic.
I agree that each lattice requires a choice of a sublattice in the GNN case, but in your approach you similarly need to make a choice of a unit cell over which you apply a convolution kernel and where you place additional nodes. As the result two approaches ultimately perform the same task of selecting a unit cell / kernel that results in the reduction of the symmetry group that recovers additional expressivity. This process does not involve any "quantum physics knowledge".

> LCN doesn't explicitly take advantage of lattice symmetries.
I believe you take advantage of translational symmetry by using CNNs + periodic padding.

> LCN uses regular kernel to convolve the augmented lattices, so it does not need to choose unit cell for convolution on different type of lattices.
I believe that a choice of a vanilla CNN kernel here is equivalent to choosing a unit cell (within which spins are interpreted differently by the network).


[1] Maron, H., Fetaya, E., Segol, N., & Lipman, Y. (2019, May). On the universality of invariant networks. In International conference on machine learning (pp. 4363-4371). PMLR.

content.title: Response to Reviewer aQ26 --- Part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback and valuable comments! We hope your concerns and questions can be addressed by our responses below.
We also made revision based on your suggestion:
- In Table 1, we change the way of denoting results. Best result in each row is denoted in bold, and LCN’s results that worse than GNN-2 but better than or same with GNN are underlined. 
- Move reference energy introduction part from appendix to main body Section 5. More detailed discussion about reference energy can be found in the answer to Q2 below.
- Add channel number and kernel size information in appendix J (Hyperparameter).


>**Q1: It is clear that GNN perform significantly better than LCN in some cases, where LCN results achieve a relative error of ~10^-2 (compared to GNN). This raises questions about whether LCN might lack the needed inductive bias that GNNs utilize in their construction. Given the stated goal of a method that relies less on prior knowledge, these negative results might show that LCNs might not yet fulfill this role.**

- Among all cases where GNN is better than LCN, the largest gain is about ~0.004, meanwhile among all cases where LCN is better than GNN, the largest gain is about ~0.005. In general, towards solving quantum many-body problems, developing a generic method is important, which need not to be tailored designed on different systems with corresponding domain knowledge. Absolutely the ultimate goal is to have a generic method without domain knowledge that can achieve best results in every cases accross all lattice systems. **As a first step towards this goal, in many cases, results of LCN are better than GNN, while in other cases results of LCN are still very competitive with GNN.** Most importantly, our work demonstrates that the quantum many-body problem on different lattices could potentially be solved in a principled way by using pure deep learning method. Unlike previous work, our method can be seamlessly applied to different lattices and different regimes, and can still achieve competitive results with other physics-informed methods. So our work has great generalizability and can also be applied to systems where prior knowlege is lacked.


>**Q2: The "reference energy" column is not clearly explained in the paper, and could cause confusion as to what it really means. I suggest clearly articulating when a reference energy is assumed to be representative of the true ground state energy and when it is simply the current best method (and in those cases, why is it fine not to directly compare to that).**

- Sorry for the confusion. We have moved the details about reference energy from Appendix B to main body Section 5 in the revision. We use the same reference energy as used in GNN paper [1]. And these reference energy are either ground truth or very tight upper bound of ground truth, so they can be seen as representative of true ground state energy. For all small systems, reference energy are the exact energy obtained from diagonalization of Hamiltonian matrix. For large systems, exact ground state energy remains unknown (due to exponential size growth of Hamiltonian matrix, diagonalization is intractable), so reference energy are derived from RBM+PP (square J2=0.5), QMC (square J2=0), DMRG (triangular and kagome) or estimates for infinite-size lattice (extrapolated from exact diagonalizations for honeycomb or from DMRG for triangular). 

Below are some more detailed explanation about above mentioned methods for deriving reference energy of large systems:
- QMC result can be treated as ground truth. And QMC can only be applied to the case J2=0, for finite J2, the model has the sign problem and cannot be simulated using QMC.
- RBM+PP is a variational wavefunction, and it combines the restricted Boltzmann machine and the pair-product wavefunction. The pair-product wavefunction has been used in physics for a long time and it is known that the pair-product wavefunction excellently captures the ground state of the Heisenberg model on a square lattice. 
- DMRG is also a variational method so the energy upbounds the ground truth. It is typically applied to a cylinder geometry, like a long ribbon, where DMRG is very accurate because the optimization is much more efficient as it does not require MCMC. 
- And some other reference energy are the estimates for infinite-size lattice, which can be treated as estimation of ground truth. Also please note that the extrapolation only gives the estimation on the energy, but does not give the wavefunction.

**Reference**\
[1] Dmitrii Kochkov, Tobias Pfaff, Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez, Peter Battaglia, and Bryan K Clark. Learning ground states of quantum hamiltonians with graph networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.06390, 2021.

content.title: Response to Reviewer aQ26 --- Part 2
content.comment:
>**Q3: Another issue is that it should be noted that the specific paper on GNN they compare against uses a completely different optimization method (IT-SWO) and not the conventional VMC -- when comparing architectures it is better to ensure all other factors remain the same. Finally, in cases where the competing method is better, it should be in bold-face to emphasize that instead of keeping the entire row in regular font.**

- Actually we tried IT-SWO, but it converges slower and cannot achieve lower energy than simple energy gradient optimization method. And there are hyperparemeters in IT-SWO which are quite sensitive and need to be tuned carefully. So we didn't adopt IT-SWO for optimization.
- Alternatively, energy gradient is an easy and straight forward way to optimize parameter (energy can be seen as loss function, so energy gradient is just simple backprogation). IT-SWO is a more advanced optimization method invented by the GNN author, which involves imaginary time evolution. According to the author of GNN, in their cases it was easier for GNN to achieve lower energy with IT-SWO than energy gradient. So in that sense, LCN is superior than GNN because LCN does not need complex optimization method to work well.
- Thanks for the suggestion about putting GNN method in bold-face when it has better performance, we've made that change in the revision.


>**Q4.1: The claim regarding LCN not needing any prior knowledge unlike previous works is a bit misleading. First, because they do incorporate prior knowledge into the architecture ...... The authors note the use of symmetry in previous works as an example of prior knowledge, but periodic symmetry is part of the LCN architecture -- so it is not clear what is different here.**

- The specific "symmetry" concept mentioned in GNN paper is different from the pariodic boundary symmetry we employed. Symmetry in GNN [1] means the lattice point group symmetry. GNN uses sublattice encoding according to lattice point group symmetry, which needs to be specifically designed for different Hamiltonian and different lattice. So it indeed needs lots of domain knowledge involved and not generic. Whereas periodic symmetry (or called periodic boundary condition) means that lattice is repeatedly tiled in the infinite space. Periodic boundary condition is a simple and intuitive fact that does not involve any quantum physics knowledge. Moreover, other domain knowledge such as Marshal sign rule, spin flip symmetry are also not used in our method.

**Reference**\
[1] Dmitrii Kochkov, Tobias Pfaff, Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez, Peter Battaglia, and Bryan K Clark. Learning ground states of quantum hamiltonians with graph networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.06390, 2021.

content.title: Response to Reviewer aQ26 --- Part 3
content.comment:
>**Q4.2: ...... and second, because some of the examples of prior knowledge they try to avoid (Marshal sign rule) are not at all addressed by their proposed method. ...... As for the use of the Marshal sign rule, while indeed other works have pointed out the difficulty of learning the sign structure without relying on some prior knowledge or heuristic, this work does not propose any arguments for why LCN helps with this challenging problem.**

- The table below shows the results comparison with CNN [1] (**also could be found in Appendix L**), which incorporates Marshal sign rule in their network. It can be seen that when J2=0, our result is same with CNN, so it means our method can learn the sign structure automatically without using Marshal sign rule. When J2=0.5, CNN result is worse than ours because the quantum system is in the most frustrated regime where prior sign rule is violated and Marshal sign rule doesn't work anymore. This also validates our methods can capture complicated sign structure in frustrated regime. 


| $6\times 6$ | J2=0 | J=0.2 | J2=0.4 | J2=0.45 | J2=0.5 | J2=0.55 | J2=0.6 | J2=0.8 | J2=1 |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| `Exact` | −0.678872 | −0.599046 | −0.529745 | N/A | −0.503810 | −0.495178 | −0.493239 | −0.586487 | −0.714360 |
| `CNN[1]` | −0.67882(1) | −0.59895(1) | −0.52936(1) | −0.51452(1) | −0.50185(1) | −0.49067(2) | −0.49023(1) | −0.58590(1) | −0.71351(1) |
| `ours` | -0.6788(1) | -0.5990(1) | -0.5295(1) | -0.5151(1) | -0.5022(2) | -0.4910(2) | -0.4840(2) | -0.5855(2) | -0.7119(3) |

- In terms of the reason why our model can capture complicated ground state, we argue that the reasons are two folds: (1) As described is Section 4, we use non-local network to explicitly capture long-range dependency, which is crutial to capture long-range spin correlation. (2) As described in Section 3.2, we use virtual vertices to augment lattice. Virtual vertices can gather and distribute the information from the original vertices, which can help increase receptive field and boost information exchange. Also, by adding virtual vertices, we can overlap the same convolution kernel in order to enable information reuse, which is crucial to capture long-range spin correlations [2]. 

**Reference**\
[1] Kenny Choo, Titus Neupert, and Giuseppe Carleo. Two-dimensional frustrated j 1- j 2 model studied with neural network quantum states. Physical Review B, 100(12):125124, 2019.\
[2] Xiao Liang, Wen-Yuan Liu, Pei-Ze Lin, Guang-Can Guo, Yong-Sheng Zhang, and Lixin He. Solving frustrated quantum many-particle models with convolutional neural networks. Physical Review B, 98(10):104426, 2018.

>**Q4.3: the locality in the convolutional layers assumes mostly short-range interactions -- a true departure from the assumption of locality would use only the non-local layers (which is really self-attention by another name)**

- Both short and long range interactions are important in learning ground state. In Heisenberg model, essentially there are two kinds of spin-spin interactions, namely nearest neighbor spin interaction and next nearest neighbor spin interaction. So it is natural and important to use convolution kernel to capture these local interactions. In addition, capturing long range spin correlation is also crutial for learning ground state of quantum spin systems especially when the system is in frustrated regime. By stacking multiple convolution layers, the network can already capture long range dependency to some extent by increasing receptive field. Beyond that, we add non-local layer on top of convolution layers to further explicitly capture long range spin correlation. 

>**Q5: Some of the hyperparameters in the experiments are missing: How many channels / kernels were used in each layer? Is the window size of the convolutional layers always 3x3? Are the number of MCMC chains equal to the batch size, or are there fewer chains and multiple samples are produced per step?**

- For all experiments, we use 3x3 convolution kernel and 64 output channels for each layer. And number of MCMC chains equals to the batch size, so one chain produces one sample per step. We've added channel number and kernel size information in Appendix J (Hyperparameter) in the revision.

content.title: Response to Reviewer maSg --- Part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your positive feedback and valuable comments! We hope your concerns and questions can be addressed by our responses below.

>**Q1: Additional modeling choices: (squeeze-and-excitation block, non-local block, SE-non-local layer) are studied in the appendix and mostly on small system size. As an exciting addition, it would be great to see whether this holds true for larger problem (108 spins) (interesting regardless of the outcome). Does this ablation depend on the underlying physics of the system? (e.g. ordered vs disordered)**

- We conduct another network architecture ablation study on 108 kagome lattice. As shown in the table below, we can still observe that adding SE-Non-Local layer to capture long-range spin dependency can help learning ground state with lower energy.

| Lattice | Size | J2 | Residual only | Residual+SE | Residual+Nonlocal | Residual+SE+Nonlocal | 
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| `Kagome` | 108 | 0 | -0.4090(5) | -0.4153(6) | -0.4161(5) | -0.4276(3) |

- And underlying physics does affect this ablation. One of the most representative ordered and disordered system is on triangular lattice. Due to the limited time, we only compare results of whether adding SE-Non-Local layers. When J2=0, system is in ordered regime and ground state for triangular lattice is easier to learn than kagome lattice, so network can achieve good result without adding SE-Non-Local layer. When J2=0.125, system is in disordered regime and ground state is much harder to learn because the system is highly frustrated and capturing long-range spin correlation becomes important. So in this case, adding SE-Non-local layer could help improve results.

| Lattice | Size | J2 | Residual only | Residual+SENonlocal | 
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| `Triangular` | 36 | 0 | -0.5600(4) | -0.5601(4) |
| `Triangular` | 36 | 0.125 | -0.5045(5) | -0.5126(6) |

content.title: Response to Reviewer maSg --- Part 2
content.comment:
>**Q2: One aspect in which I disagree with the authors is their structural comparison with graph neural networks. Both the GNN and the proposed LCN options attempt to take advantage of the lattice symmetries to make the ansatz more suitable for the problem at hand. For a general lattice symmetry this comes at a price of limited representability (assuming standard CNN-based or graph network based implementations) which in general hurts the variational energies. Both GNN and the proposed LCN address this tension by selecting a sublattice, which in GNN is encoded as additional input features and in the LCN case is determined by the choice of the unit cell for the underlying convolutions (both uses the same heuristic that does not involve any “domain knowledge”).**

- Thanks for the valuable question. First, since GNN cannot capture structure information naturally, so it need to explicitly design sublattice encoding as auxiliary input according to lattice point group symmetry. And in pratice GNN sublattice encoding need to be specifically designed for different Hamiltonian (different J2 value) and different lattice types, so it indeed need quantum physics knowledge involved and not generic.
- LCN doesn't explicitly take advantage of lattice symmetries and doesn't select sublattice. LCN applied the exact same method to augment differet kinds of original lattices with virtual vertices to and uses regular kernel to convolve the augmented lattices, so it does not need to choose unit cell for convolution on different type of lattices. Convolution kernel has different learnable weights so it enables different kernels to capture different local structure information automatically through end-to-end training. But we did also tried to design special kernel to capture different local structures on original lattice as shown in Appendix E. But in practice we found regular kernel consistently outperform special kernel as shown in Table 3. The reason is that special kernel is hard to share weights and there's less overlap between same special kernel, and these can be overcomed by lattice augmentation and regular kernel. More detailed discussion can be found in Section 5 `Kernel Design Comparison` paragraph.

>**Q3: \
(1) Related work: “to augment system configurations in order to respect underlying quantum symmetry” - I don’t think graph neural networks have any “quantum symmetries”, am I misunderstanding?\
(2) Introduction: “suffers entanglement problems”\
(3) Consider switching network ablation study (ideally extended :) ) from the appendix and reproduction of the GNN ablation study, since the former is new and provides an interesting piece of evidence.**

(1) Conventional graph neural networks doesn't have quantum symmetry, but sublattice encoding is designed to capture quantum symmetry and is appended to the input of GNN.\
(2) Tensor network is a specific class of variational ansatz that can only express wavefunction that has low entanglement entropy, in other words, not too complicated, while neural network states do not have this limitation.\
(3) Thanks for the suggestion, we've switched these two part in the revision.

>**Q4: \
(1) Variational principle in quantum mechanics (Lanczos method has been shown up to ~48). \
(2) Background and related work: “all combinations of spins form a basis” (remove “a set”)?**

- Thanks for pointing out. We've already changed that in the revision. 

>**Q5: It is conceivable that the results could be reproduced solely from the paper, but a commitment from the authors to release the code upon acceptance would be a big plus.**

- Yes, we will release code upon acceptance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer xp3P
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback. We hope your concerns and questions can be addressed by our responses below.

>**Q1: Adapting the usual CNNs to non-square lattices for replacing graph neural networks is an interesting idea. But a linear transformation should easily transfer a non-square lattice to the square one. Unless I miss something, the problem seems to be easy. The authors should convince the readers why this simple approach does not work.**

- Thanks reviewer for raising this question. Sorry for causing the confusion. The reviewer's misunderstanding might comes from the sentence in the paper: "Triangular lattices can be viewed as sheared square lattices where every unit cell of the square lattice undergoes the same affine transformation." 
- The reason we say triangular lattice can be seen as sheard square lattice undergoes affine transformation is that we want to make it more clear that vertices in triangular lattice can be one-to-one mapped to vertices on a grid-like data, so regular convolution can be directly used. But this is not always the case, not even for the triangular lattice. The reasons are: (1) lattice with finite vertices usually have irregular boundaries, for example, in Figure 2 the original lattice boundary does not necessary to be a parallelogram, it can be a hexagon, so boundary alignment is needed otherwise convolution cannot be used on the boundaries (2) For honeycomb and kagome lattice, they have multiple repetitive local structures instead of one grid-like substructure, so they cannot be directly seen as grid-like data. (If use the reviewer's word, in these cases simple "linear transformation" do not work.)
- In order to use regular convolution kernel on different lattices, we propose a set of operations to convert non-square lattices to grid-like augmented lattices in a principled way. The most important operation is lattice augmentation that adds virtual vertices on the original lattice. **The benefit of adding virtual vertices are two folds as mentioned in the last paragraph of Section 3.2**. First, it can gather and distribute the information from the original vertices, which can help increase receptive fields and boost information exchange. Second, we can overlap the same convolution kernel in order to enable information reuse, which is crucial to capture long-range spin correlations [1]. Besides that, we also propose lattice convolution network that involves attention mechanism to capture long-range spin correlation in quantum spin system. In summary, lattice augmentation and lattice convolution network together achieve high wavefunction expressivity and solve quantum-many body problem on different lattices in a principled way.

**Reference**\
[1] Xiao Liang, Wen-Yuan Liu, Pei-Ze Lin, Guang-Can Guo, Yong-Sheng Zhang, and Lixin He. Solving frustrated quantum many-particle models with convolutional neural networks. Physical Review B, 98(10):104426, 2018.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper investigates application of neural networks based on lattice convolutions as variational ansatz for a quantum many body problem on a set of lattices (including non-square variations such as triangular, honeycomb and kagome). Authors test their approach on commonly studied Heisenberg models with up-to second nearest neighbor interactions. They compare their results to other methods compatible with non-square geometry such as graph neural networks finding their method competitive.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* Authors provide results on a range of model problems and obtain competitive variational energies
* The proposed method compares favorably to relevant baselines
* Proposed architecture should be able to utilize hardware accelerators well

Weaknesses:
* Additional modeling choices: (squeeze-and-excitation block, non-local block, SE-non-local layer) are studied in the appendix and mostly on small system size. As an exciting addition, it would be great to see whether this holds true for larger problem (108 spins) (interesting regardless of the outcome). Does this ablation depend on the underlying physics of the system? (e.g. ordered vs disordered)
* The primary difference with respect to a GNN baseline is misrepresented/obscured (see main review for details)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written clearly and provides enough details to understand the setup and the model being tested. Authors cite relevant works and describe concepts that might be new to a general audience interested in the topic. It is conceivable that the results could be reproduced solely from the paper, but a commitment from the authors to release the code upon acceptance would be a big plus.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall a solid paper that achieves good results on a set of challenging benchmark problems (that are still an open research topic). The proposed method would be of value to the research community interested in applying machine learning to problems in many body quantum physics, as well as could be of interest to a wider ML for science audience.

The paper features good results and authors make logical & clear efforts to support the claims. There are a few additional ablation studies that could improve the paper from a physics insight standpoint: (on small system size on Kagome lattice including nonlocal information seems to noticeably help - does this still hold for larger system sizes?)

One aspect in which I disagree with the authors is their structural comparison with graph neural networks. Both the GNN and the proposed LCN options attempt to take advantage of the lattice symmetries to make the ansatz more suitable for the problem at hand. For a general lattice symmetry this comes at a price of limited representability (assuming standard CNN-based or graph network based implementations) which in general hurts the variational energies. Both GNN and the proposed LCN address this tension by selecting a sublattice, which in GNN is encoded as additional input features and in the LCN case is determined by the choice of the unit cell for the underlying convolutions (both uses the same heuristic that does not involve any “domain knowledge”). The real advantage of the proposed method, from my perspective, is that the paper uses regular convolutions that are likely to be much more efficient on modern hardware than message passing steps, enabling faster iteration and better variational energies given the same compute budget.

I’m also a believer that statements of “primacy” and “novelty” at ICLR submissions are generally not load bearing and should be discouraged.

Minor comments, confusions, suggestions:
* Related work: “to augment system configurations in order to respect underlying quantum symmetry” - I don’t think graph neural networks have any “quantum symmetries”, am I misunderstanding?
* Introduction: “suffers entanglement problems”
* Consider switching network ablation study (ideally extended :) ) from the appendix and reproduction of the GNN ablation study, since the former is new and provides an interesting piece of evidence.

Super minor nits:
* Variational principle in quantum mechanics (Lanczos method has been shown up to ~48)
* Background and related work: “all combinations of spins form a basis” (remove “a set”)?

content.summary_of_the_paper: In the context of Variational Monte Carlo for finding the ground state of quantum many-body systems, convolutional neural networks have proven to be a powerful ansatz for solving square lattices. This paper proposes a method for extending ConvNet quantum states to non-square lattices by projecting them onto square lattices with non-uniform paddings to fill the holes in the projection. Prior works on neural networks for non-square lattices have focused on graph neural networks instead, which relied on hand-crafted features to encode the geometry of the lattice. By building on the success of ConvNets, this work aims to offer a simpler, more principled approach. The experimental results on the challenging J1-J2 Heisenberg model demonstrate that the proposed method can perform as well or better in most cases without relying on any hand-crafted features.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

* Simpler more principled novel method that builds on the power of ConvNets, instead of trying to adapt GNN to less conventional settings, and using less external knowledge on the given problem. This could be crucial when tackling more intricate systems without the need to carefully tune the method to them.

* Clearly written.

* Extensive experiments demonstrating that in *most* (but not all) cases lattice ConvNets (LCN) can achieve better accuracy than the competing GNN approach.

Weaknesses:

* It is clear that GNN perform significantly better than LCN in some cases, where LCN results achieve a relative error of ~10^-2 (compared to GNN). This raises questions about whether LCN might lack the needed inductive bias that GNNs utilize in their construction. Given the stated goal of a method that relies less on prior knowledge, these negative results might show that LCNs might not yet fulfill this role.

* There are a few issues with the presentation of the results. For one, the "reference energy" column is a bit problematic and requires more careful discussion. Specifically, in many cases there is not yet a consensus that a correct estimate of the energy is presently available (e.g., for J1/J2 = 0.5 for 10x10 lattice), and so the last column in some cases is not really a reference that can be used to evaluate how well LCN solve the task, but is in fact a competing neural network that solves it more effectively. Another issue is that it should be noted that the specific paper on GNN they compare against uses a completely different optimization method (IT-SWO) and not the conventional VMC -- when comparing architectures it is better to ensure all other factors remain the same. Finally, in cases where the competing method is better, it should be in bold-face to emphasize that instead of keeping the entire row in regular font.

* The claim regarding LCN not needing any prior knowledge unlike previous works is a bit misleading. First, because they do incorporate prior knowledge into the architecture, and second, because some of the examples of prior knowledge they try to avoid (Marshal sign rule) are not at all addressed by their proposed method. Namely, the locality in the convolutional layers assumes mostly short-range interactions -- a true departure from the assumption of locality would use only the non-local layers (which is really self-attention by another name). The authors note the use of symmetry in previous works as an example of prior knowledge, but periodic symmetry is part of the LCN architecture -- so it is not clear what is different here. As for the use of the Marshal sign rule, while indeed other works have pointed out the difficulty of learning the sign structure without relying on some prior knowledge or heuristic, this work does not propose any arguments for why LCN helps with this challenging problem.

* Some of the hyperparameters in the experiments are missing: How many channels / kernels were used in each layer? Is the window size of the convolutional layers always 3x3? Are the number of MCMC chains equal to the batch size, or are there fewer chains and multiple samples are produced per step?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The method and general problem are clearly described. The "reference energy" column is not clearly explained in the paper, and could cause confusion as to what it really means. I suggest clearly articulating when a reference energy is assumed to be representative of the true ground state energy and when it is simply the current best method (and in those cases, why is it fine not to directly compare to that).

Quality: Some of the claims in the paper are not well supported, as previously discussed regarding the claim that LCN does not rely on any prior knowledge. Moreover, the results and the comparison to prior works are not always framed correctly.

Novelty: The proposed method is definitely novel. It is addressing the non-trivial problem of extending convolutional networks to non-square lattices, instead of relying on more complicated solutions that require more careful calibration to each instance.

Reproducibility: With the exception of a few missing hyper-parameters of the architectural model and other very technical details, the work should be very reproducible, and the mentioned exception could be easily addressed in a revision.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the proposed method is novel and offers a principled solution to a non-trivial problem, the presentation of the results and prior works, as well as the lack of support for the core arguments leads me to recommend rejecting it. It could be that with a major revision addressing the presentation issues, and perhaps improving some of the results that showed GNN to be superior, the paper could be accepted.

content.title: Lattice Convolutional Networks for Learning Ground States of Quantum Many-Body Systems
content.abstract: Deep learning methods have been shown to be effective in representing ground-state wave functions of quantum many-body systems. Existing methods use convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for square lattices due to their image-like structures. For non-square lattices, existing method uses graph neural network (GNN) in which structure information is not precisely captured, thereby requiring additional hand-crafted sublattice encoding. In this work, we propose lattice convolutions in which a set of proposed operations are used to convert non-square lattices into grid-like augmented lattices on which regular convolution can be applied. Based on the proposed lattice convolutions, we design lattice convolutional networks (LCN) that use self-gating and attention mechanisms. Experimental results show that our method achieves performance on par or better than the GNN method on spin 1/2 $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model over the square, honeycomb, triangular, and kagome lattices while without using hand-crafted encoding.
